questions.q: Where should a real capacity forecast start, according to this lesson?
options: From a round number chosen by rounding up last quarter's peak
From the vendor's marketed maximum throughput for the hardware in use
From a competitor's publicly reported traffic figures
From the organization's historical monitoring data — request rate, utilization, and storage growth already captured in the monitoring stack
questions.explain: Capacity forecasting starts with the organization's own historical time-series data from its monitoring stack, not a memory-based guess or a borrowed number.

questions.q: What is the practical risk of fitting a linear growth model to data that is actually compounding (exponential)?
options: The forecast looks accurate for a while, then the real curve pulls away from the straight line and capacity runs out faster than planned
There is no risk; linear and compounding models always produce the same forecast
It guarantees the forecast will overestimate future need indefinitely
It only affects storage metrics, never compute or request-rate metrics
questions.explain: Compounding growth increases by a roughly constant percentage, so its absolute increment grows over time. A linear fit tracks the early data reasonably well, then underestimates badly as the real curve accelerates away from the straight line.

questions.q: Why does a sound capacity forecast include a confidence band rather than a single point estimate?
options: Because point estimates are illegal under most compliance frameworks
Because a confidence band removes the need to ever re-forecast
Because no forecast projected into the future is exact, and the uncertainty widens the further out the projection goes
Because confidence bands are a formatting convention with no real meaning
questions.explain: Forecast uncertainty is a normal, expected statistical property that grows with distance from the historical data — a trend line alone hides that uncertainty, while a confidence band makes it visible so you can plan against it.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which point on the forecast's confidence band should drive an actual capacity-planning decision?
options: The lower bound of the band, to avoid over-provisioning
The upper bound of the band at the planning horizon, not the midpoint
Whichever number is cheapest to provision
The average of the upper and lower bounds from the prior year's forecast only
questions.explain: Planning to the midpoint gives roughly even odds of running out of capacity right when it matters. Planning to the upper bound of a reasonable confidence interval is what actually protects against the forecast being wrong on the high side.

questions.q: Why can a technically accurate forecast still fail to prevent a capacity shortfall, according to this lesson's discussion of lead time?
options: Because headroom buffers eliminate the need to consider lead time at all
Because lead time only applies to on-premises data centers, never to cloud environments
Because forecasts are only ever produced once per company's lifetime

Because accuracy is irrelevant if there isn't enough lead time to turn the forecast into actual provisioned capacity — e.g., quota increases or hardware procurement that take longer than the forecast horizon allows
questions.explain: A forecast is only useful if there's enough lead time to act on it. If provisioning actions (quota increases, reserved capacity, hardware procurement) take longer than the forecast horizon, the organization is structurally unable to react in time regardless of forecast accuracy.
